name: VAT
seoDesc: VAT: work out your result from the VAT rate. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary:
The VAT calculator returns your result from the 2 fields on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below.

It is built for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the VAT calculator work?
sections.html:
The VAT calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the VAT rate.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in percent. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as add VAT and exclude VAT. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the VAT calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Amount=gross price ÷ (VAT rate + 1)
Amount=net price × (VAT rate + 1)
Tax amount=amount × VAT rate
Tax amount=-amount + gross price
Tax amount=net price × VAT rate
Tax amount=amount − net price

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take VAT rate = 10 % and Gross price = 10. The calculator returns Amount = 9, Tax amount = 1 and Net price = 8.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Amount = 9, Tax amount = 1 and Net price = 8 should be roughly the size you expected from VAT rate = 10 % and Gross price = 10.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • %, opening in percent
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The VAT calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the VAT rate — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the VAT calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the VAT rate, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter amount in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Amount opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Amount = 9. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the VAT calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
